The excerpt provides general evidence that atmospheric oxygen during selective laser melting can substantially affect material quality and mechanical behavior, but it does not report a complete 100–2000 ppm comparison for AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, or 7xxx aluminum alloys, nor does it specifically quantify hydrogen porosity or oxide inclusions for those alloys. For alloyed steel and stainless steel, higher oxygen promotes larger melt-pool volumes and balling, degrading surface quality; balling can be reduced by maintaining low oxygen. In Ti-6Al-4V, increased oxygen raises ultimate tensile strength but reduces fatigue resistance, while oxygen and nitrogen uptake causes embrittlement, higher strength, and lower elongation. For AlCu5MnCdVA, low oxygen (20 ppm) produced higher tensile strength and elongation than 200 ppm, and low oxygen increased density in tungsten alloys. The authors emphasize that oxygen effects on AlSi10Mg had received limited attention and therefore investigate controlled oxygen concentration during LPBF/SLM, including tensile properties of bulk AlSi10Mg and quasi-static compression of primitive, gyroid, and diamond TPMS lattices. ## pqac-00000007

From text 'pauzon2019theprocessatmosphere pages 22-25'.

C Pauzon. The process atmosphere as a parameter in the laser-powder bed fusion process. Unknown journal, 2019.

The excerpt provides general mechanisms relevant to oxygen levels around 100–2000 ppm during LPBF, but it does not report alloy-specific results for AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, or 7xxx aluminum alloys, nor does it quantify effects on spatter, fatigue life, hydrogen porosity, or mechanical properties. Increasing oxygen partial pressure can increase oxygen adsorption and dissolution at the melt-pool interface, although evaporation of metal atoms and existing oxides may hinder adsorption. Dissolved oxygen can remain in solution or form oxides at the melt-pool surface or inside the material; convection, including Marangoni flow, affects its distribution. Because oxygen solubility generally decreases during solidification, gas porosity may form. Higher oxygen activity also promotes oxide-scale growth on reactive powder particles and stabilizes many oxides. The cited process example indicates that reducing oxygen from 2% to 0.1% prevented balling in 316L, attributed to reduced melt-pool oxidation and improved wettability. The excerpt identifies approximately 1000 ppm residual oxygen as relatively high for oxide stability, but does not establish direct trends for aluminum-alloy porosity, oxide inclusions, hydrogen-related pores, spatter, fatigue performance, or strength and ductility.

Abstract:
This article explores the main mechanisms that can generate damage in polymers and polymer-based materials used for hydrogen storage and distribution infrastructures. All of these mechanisms are driven by the permeability process that is enhanced by the operating temperature and pressure conditions. Hydrogen storage and delivery systems typically work under high pressure and a relatively wide range of temperatures, especially during the filling and emptying processes. Therefore, it is of great interest to better understand how this phenomenon can influence the integrity of polymer-based hydrogen infrastructures in order to avoid catastrophic events and to better design/investigate new optimized solutions. The first part of this paper discusses the main storage and delivery solutions for gas and liquid hydrogen. Then, the physics of the permeability is investigated with a focus on the effect of pressure and temperature on the integrity of polymers working in a hydrogen environment. Finally, the main mechanisms that mostly induce damage in polymers operating in a hydrogen environment and that influence their mechanical properties are explored and discussed. Particular focus was placed on the rapid gas decompression and aging phenomena. In addition, some of the limits that still exist for a reliable design of polymer-based storage and delivery systems for hydrogen are pointed out.

EPDM is not listed in this excerpt, so no direct Viton-versus-EPDM comparison can be supported. The excerpt also does not discuss vacuum-chamber outgassing rates of FKM/Viton or aluminum surfaces; it concerns gas permeation through O-rings and storage drift in atmospheric sampling flasks. Abstract:
Among oxygen sensors, types such as polymer-, ceramic-, or carbon-based ones may be distinguished. Particular interest in semiconductor metal oxide (SMO) sensors has recently been observed. This is due to their easy fabrication process, high control over the final product (dopants, posttreatment, etc.), and high concentration of oxygen vacancies, by which they show significant changes in electrical properties when exposed to analyte. In this review, different types of sensors are described and categorized. Importantly, their limitations, challenges and principles of sensing mechanism are also discussed, wherein attention is primarily paid to semiconductor metal oxide (SMO) oxygen sensors. This comprehensive review provides an in-depth analysis of the existing literature on planar SMO oxygen sensors, focusing on various materials, fabrication techniques, and sensing mechanisms. It also critically assesses the challenges and limitations in current research, offering insights into future directions for developing highly efficient and reliable sensors. Currently, most oxygen resistive sensors are a few micrometers thick and operate at high temperatures, which leads to high power consumption. To highlight importance of this topic, a market overview is also presented.

This study presents a resistive sensor concept based on Barium Iron Tantalate (BFT) to measure the oxygen stoichiometry in exhaust gases of combustion processes. The BFT sensor film was deposited on the substrate by the Powder Aerosol Deposition (PAD) method. In initial laboratory experiments, the sensitivity to pO2 in the gas phase was analyzed. The results agree with the defect chemical model of BFT materials that suggests the formation of holes h• by filling oxygen vacancies VO•• in the lattice at higher oxygen partial pressures pO2. The sensor signal was found to be sufficiently accurate and to have low time constants with changing oxygen stoichiometry. Further investigations on reproducibility and cross-sensitivities to typical exhaust gas species (CO2, H2O, CO, NO, …) confirmed a robust sensor signal that was hardly affected by other gas components. The sensor concept was also tested in real engine exhausts for the first time. The experimental data showed that the air-fuel ratio can be monitored by measuring the resistance of the sensor element, including partial and full-load operation modes. Furthermore, no signs of inactivation or aging during the test cycles were observed for the sensor film. Overall, a promising first data set was obtained in engine exhausts and therefore the BFT system is a possible cost-effective alternative concept to existing commercial sensors in the future. Moreover, the integration of other sensitive films for multi-gas sensor purposes might be an attractive field for future studies.

The excerpt directly compares a zirconia-based lambda oxygen probe with an electrochemical oxygen sensor in LPBF. It concludes that the electrochemical sensor provides more reliable oxygen-variation measurements. The lambda probe is described as a solid ceramic electrolyte sensor, typically yttria-stabilized zirconia with platinum electrodes, operating at approximately 700 °C. Its output can be affected by hydrogen, carbon monoxide, nitric oxide, and hydrocarbons because these species may oxidize on the hot sensor head. In particular, hydrogen—likely originating from water vapor, humid powder, machine surfaces, or leaks—causes the lambda probe to underestimate oxygen. During one build, a 50 ppm oxygen increase recorded by the lambda probe corresponded to a 700 ppm increase measured by the electrochemical cell. The excerpt states that electrochemical cells do not exhibit the lambda probe’s cross-sensitivity. It also reports that the electrochemical sensor measured an oxygen increase of approximately 1.7 ppm O2/min over seven hours. However, the passage does not provide numerical accuracy specifications across the 1–1000 ppm range, response-time data, poisoning results for metal condensates or silicones, or a detailed calibration procedure for LPBF. It only indicates that improved oxygen control would benefit from the electrochemical sensor.

Sleight Halley, Kannan Pasupathikovil Ramaiyan, Lok-kun Tsui, and Fernando Garzon. A review of zirconia oxygen, nox, and mixed potential gas sensors – history and current trends. This article has 81 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not provide numerical accuracy, response-time data, or calibration procedures for zirconia oxygen sensors in the 1–1000 ppm range, nor does it discuss LPBF additive-manufacturing calibration, poisoning specifically by metal condensates or silicones, or hydrogen cross-sensitivity. It does establish important operating limitations and alternatives. Conventional zirconia Lambda/Nernst sensors are intended for near-stoichiometric air–fuel control and their voltage saturates outside approximately lambda 0.95–1.05, so they are unsuitable for broad oxygen-concentration measurement.       The main carriage is the main mechanical system built around a stainless steel frame and
granite base, and houses the build bed, powder feed, recoating mechanisms, and most major
mechanical and motion components.  The carriage frame can be removed from the vacuum
chamber by rolling along caster wheels on vee and flat tracks, and onto the external, mobile
carriage dolly, which has similar tracks.  The carriage dolly includes a winch and strap that
connects to the main carriage to pull the carriage out of the vacuum chamber.

      The vacuum chamber, designed for medium vacuum (0.1 Pa or 10-3 torr) operation,
provides vacuum purging prior to backfilling with nitrogen or argon inert gas. This provides faster
means to reduce oxygen levels compared to simply purging with inert gas. The vacuum chamber
also provides access panels on all sides for cable and hose feedthroughs and user access to the
build area and carriage underside. This also provides flexibility for incorporating future custom
panels with ports or feedthroughs for newer or varying instrumentation or research projects.

      The optics tower contains the main optical components to control and guide the heating
laser, and divert back-emitted melt pool radiation to different modules.  Pulling vacuum on the
chamber will cause it to deflect, therefore the optics tower and fixed optical components are
mechanically de-coupled from the chamber, and coupled to the granite by sitting on the optics
tower bridge (not shown in Figure 1). The optics tower and internal components are vacuum
compatible and can be purged, however a broadband window can be inserted between the optics


                                             1148tower and main chamber to isolate the optics tower from vacuum. The optics tower contains the
galvanometric (galvo) scanner mirrors, removable beamsplitter/reflector (RSR), mirrors etc. for
the laser delivery path, the process monitoring path, or the metrology beam path. The back-emitted
radiation from the melt pool is switched between the process control module or the TEMPS module
by a manually swapped, kinematically mounted RSR accessed by opening the top lid of the tower.
Either a broadband reflector, or laser-line reflector is exchanged in the RSR position to switch
operation between the process control module, or the TEMPS module.  The optics tower is
kinematically mounted to the optics bridge, which is rigidly attached to the granite base, however
it is mechanically isolated from the vacuum chamber through a sealed, vacuum gasket flange.

      The process control module sits atop the chamber adjacent to the optics tower, and is the
heart of the AMMT process monitoring for additive manufacturing research.  This module is
essentially an enclosed optical breadboard which contains the laser fiber, beam expander, negative
lens, and other bending mirrors or windows for the laser injection beam path to the optics tower.
When the broadband reflector (700 nm to 1100 nm) is installed in the RSR position within the
optics tower, this module also receives the back-emitted radiation from the melt pool which is
further filtered to the 700 nm to 900 nm range with another beamsplitter. This 700 nm to 900 nm
bandwidth can then be further split to various optical sensors, including high speed imagers or
photodetectors. The process monitoring module provides extra space for these different optical
configurations and instruments to use the back-emitted light for researching various co-axial melt
pool monitoring methods.

      The TEMPS module (not shown in Figure 1) contains the toroidal mirror, folding mirrors,
mirrored  field  stop, and other components  to support  spectral emissivity and  reflectance
measurements. The mirrored field stop allows back emitted radiation to pass through an aperture
to various instruments, while reflecting the surrounding image to a high speed thermal imager.
This allows the imager to ‘see’ the thermal field around the aperture, and help discern the relative
location on or near the melt pool that is passed through the aperture to the sensors. TEMPS
instruments include Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectrometer, visible array spectrograph,
and filtered radiometers. Although not in the same physical location as the TEMPS module located
behind the chamber but not shown in Figure 1, an in-situ hemispherical reflectometer (also not
shown in Figure 1) used only for TEMPS operation will be incorporated within the build chamber,

systematic approach to error identification and tabulation. A guiding principle in precision

## 2. pauzon2019theprocessatmosphere pages 11-15 (Context ID: pqac-00000027)

tools comes hand in hand with the identification of influential process parameters.

Inert gases play a significant role along the process chain of the L-PBF process, from the feed material
production to the final heat treatment, through the laser process itself. For example, they are involved
during the powder gas atomization (GA) to protect the melted ingots from oxidation, and as highly
pressurized gas streams to produce the metal droplets which solidify into relatively spherical particles
upon cooling. Besides, there is the inert gas or the atmosphere under which the produced powder is
subsequently packed, shipped, stored and handled and which may affect its degradation. Finally, inert
gases are also involved in some of the post-processing steps such as heat treatment and hot isostatic
pressing (HIP).

The gas as a process parameter has, to great extent, been overlooked in favour of the material and laser-
related parameters such as the powder flowability, the laser power, the scanning speed, etc. As a result,
limited understanding of the effect of the gas properties on the properties of the produced material has
been gathered.

Still, within the L-PBF research community, there is no doubt that the protective atmosphere is necessary
for several reasons: to limit the oxidation of the material, both the produced material and the used
feedstock, to ensure a clean laser path by removing process by-products from the interaction area, and
finally, to remove the heat generated at the melt pool. The short interaction time between the laser and
the material yield a dynamic melt pool, solidifying rapidly. As a result, the above presented roles of the
gas are co-dependent. Custom practice includes the use of argon and/or nitrogen. Most of the equipment
manufacturers provide material specific guidelines, essentially limiting the use of nitrogen for materials
sensitive to nitrogen pick-up, such as Ti-6Al-4V alloy.


                                         31.1. Research objectives

The research objective of the presented work is to understand the effect of the process atmosphere
characteristics on the stability of the L-PBF process by studying the defect generation and produced
material properties. Specific addressed questions are defined as follows:

     -  What is the effect of the atmosphere purity on the properties of 316L stainless steel?
     -  What is the effect of the standard gases – argon or nitrogen – on the properties of 316L stainless
         steel?
     -  What is the effect of argon-helium gas mixtures on the process stability and properties of
       Ti-6Al-4V?





                                         4Chapter 2: Metal Additive Manufacturing

As opposed to traditional subtractive techniques, AM consists in adding material layer upon layer,
instead of removing it, to produce parts of complex geometries. Described by the ASTM F2792 [1], AM
processes can be divided into seven main groups of technologies:

     -   binder jetting
     -   directed energy deposition
     -   material extrusion
     -   material jetting
     -   powder bed fusion
     -   sheet lamination
     -   vat photopolymerization

AM covers a wide range of materials and opportunities to produce complex near-net shape parts of
various sizes. In this work, the focus is on metal L-PBF.

2.1.  Laser - Powder Bed Fusion

2.1.1.  Forewords

Recently, AM and more particularly L-PBF, has drawn significant attention from the society, industrial
and scientific communities. Among its advantages lies the production of customized goods, for instance
tailored medical implants. The possibility to create complex features comes in hand with the new
approach to design towards functionality. This is interesting for the aerospace and energy sectors, and
the development of new lightweight components, sometimes replacing a prior assembly of parts. For
example, Siemens produced an optimized gas turbine burner in one part instead of 13 individual pieces
and 18 welds in its Swedish facilities (Finspång) [3]. Other benefits of the technology are the material
utilization since minimum to no machining is required and the powder can be re-used to some extent.
For this reason, the technology has been successfully adopted by the industry. As highlighted by
Wohler’s report 2017, the sales of metal AM systems increased significantly, from about 200 units in
2012 to 950 units in 2016 [4].

Within the AM community, Sweden places itself as a world leader of the metal powder production, with
a well-established know-how in Powder Metallurgy (PM). Still, as the sales of metal AM systems
increase, effort has to be brought to cope with the rising demand for metal powder volume and variety
of available materials. In this context, understanding and development of the L-PBF process for specific
material classes is of significant importance.

2.1.2.  Principle

The L-PBF uses a laser as a heat source to selectively melt subsequent layers of powder and produce a
part. Figure 1 displays the L-PBF process cycle, which can be divided into the pre-processing, the
building of the part, and the post-processing. The powder recycling is often performed to enhance the
material use.

The pre-processing consists of the data preparation of the part to be built. The design of the part can be
created by a computer-aided design software (CAD). From the CAD file, an STL (STereo-Lithography)
file is generated. The latter is a triangular representation into small surface elements of the design, which
has to be placed within the virtual built volume (corresponding to the volume over the build plate), and
further oriented, scaled, etc. This is generally done using a supplementary software. The manufacturers
software allows to define the process parameters such as the layer thickness and then to slice the design
accordingly. The information is gathered in a process file containing the necessary data, which is sent
to the L-PBF machine. Before the process starts, the machine must be prepared by an operator, who
will, for example, load the powder and conduct several adjustments.

                                         5The L-PBF machines usually consist of the following elements: an optical system (laser and scanning
system), a powder dispenser platform, a building platform on which a build plate is mounted, a powder
collector platform and a recoater to apply the powder, see Figure 1. These elements are placed into a
volume called the process chamber. Right before the process is initiated, final adjustments of the level
of the build plate relatively to the recoater are made. After the spreading of a thin layer of powder, the
required process atmosphere (purity, composition) is established, typically by flushing the gas chamber
with the process gas. The process is now able to start. The laser is turned on and will selectively scan
some areas of the build plate, corresponding to the bulk of the input design. When this step is completed,
the laser is turned off. The building platform is dropped by a layer thickness while the powder dispenser
platform is raised. The recoater will rake the powder which is now above its level and spread it over the
lowered build plate. The excess of the powder will be brought to the collector platform, which is also
lowered during the process. The laser is turned on again to scan the following layer. This is repeated
until the complete height of the part is reached.

Afterwards, the operator can open the process chamber and dismount the build plate, on which the parts
are located, from the building platform. Some post-processing is necessary to remove the part from the
plate and to achieve the possible parts requirements in terms of strength, surface quality, etc. Heat
treatments can be applied for different purposes, e.g. stress relief, annealing, reaching a required
microstructure, etc.

To start the next process, the machine has to be prepared again following a similar procedure. The
powder accumulated in the collector and on the building platform has to be sieved prior to be re-used,
to ensure a consistent particle size distribution (PSD).





Figure 1: Process cycle of L-PBF.

Process atmosphere generation

When the L-PBF machine is prepared for a building sequence, the operator closes the chamber door. As
a result, the initial atmosphere in the process chamber is the same as the ambient workshop atmosphere
(i.e. similar humidity and composition). The gas will enter the chamber from an inlet which is a
distributor that splits the main gas flow, ideally into a homogeneous flow covering the build plate
towards an  outlet. The design of the gas  inlet  is an active development  activity  for machine
manufacturers to assure a homogeneous laminar gas flow over the whole build plate.

              Introduction




In this chapter, the background and context of the thesis are outlined, providing the founda-
tion necessary to understand the problem under investigation. The problem statement is pre-
sented together with the motivations for the study and its objectives. Furthermore, the scope
and limitations of the thesis are defined to clarify the boundaries within which the thesis has
been conducted.


1.1  Background


The use of additive manufacturing (AM) solutions to produce metal products has increased
significantly in recent years within industries such as automotive, aerospace, and medtech, due
to lower energy consumption, shorter lead times, and improved material efficiency (RISE, 20

2.1.2  Review of Existing Solutions


To gain a better overview of similar solutions available on the market, a review of existing solu-
tions was conducted. Relevant solutions were identified through structured searches in scientific
databases, company websites, and technical reports using keywords related to the relevant tech-
nical areas.


2.1.3  Patent Analysis


A patent search was conducted on Espacenet with a focus on relevant technical areas. The aim
was to establish a state-of-the-art overview and to identify technical solutions that could serve
as inspiration in the concept development phase. The search was thus used primarily to broaden
the technical reference space and to capture less conventional solution principles that otherwise
risk being overlooked.


2.1.4  Technical Analysis


To further develop an understanding of the system, a technical analysis was conducted. This
involved reviewing relevant standards and applying equations for key parameters that affect
system performance. The analysis provided a foundation for evaluating solutions and identifying
critical factors influencing the development of a solution.


2.2  System Requirements


After the necessary background information had been collected, it was structured and used as a
basis for developing potential solutions to the problem. This was first done by decomposing the
system into a functional tree to achieve a clear overview of its main functions and subsystems.



6                                                                                         2. Methods


Subsequently, all requirements and wishes were structured into a requirements specification,
which served as the foundation for the subsequent development phase.


2.2.1  Functional Analysis


To gain a clearer understanding of the overall system, a functional analysis was conducted. A
hierarchical function tree was developed, with the main system function at the top level. This
was subsequently decomposed into sub-functions, which were further broken down until all
relevant system functions were identified. The scope of this thesis was then highlighted within
the function tree. This approach ensured that all relevant functions were considered during the
project.


2.2.2  Requirement Specification


Based on the information and knowledge gathered during the preliminary study phase, a re-
quirements specification was developed. The specification systematically documented all iden-
tified requirements and desired characteristics. For each criterion, the following information
was defined: name, description, importance, value, unit, verification method, and source. This
structure ensured traceability, clarity, and measurability throughout the complete process.

The value specifies the level required for a criterion to be considered fulfilled. Importance was
assigned only to desired characteristics and rated on a scale from 1 to 5, where 5 represented the
highest importance for meeting customer expectations.

The requirements specification was treated as a living document and served as a guideline
throughout the project, forming the basis for design decisions and concept evaluation. As the
project progressed, new criteria could be added as they were identified, and existing criteria
were revised or removed if they were no longer considered relevant.


2.3  Evaluation of Today’s Solution


Since the aim of the project was to adapt the design to work as a suitable AM build chamber
for larger build volumes, not everything had to be improved. Therefore, an initial evaluation
of today’s enclosure was required to state which areas required improvement and which were
already sufficient. The evaluation was primarily based on existing CAD models and data sheets
to identify components that could pose potential risks to fulfilling the defined requirements.
Additionally, several calculations and static simulations were performed to assess whether the
existing solution met these criteria.



                                                                           72. Methods


2.4  Concept Development


Once all groundwork was complete, the process of developing the enclosure components that
required improvement began.  This was first done by generating concepts, which were then
evaluated and screened in order to identify the optimal solutions.


2.4.1  Concept Generation


Based on the areas needing improvement, the project group held brainstorming sessions to gen-
erate potential solutions for each problem area. The brainstorming was conducted in an open,
non-judgmental manner, in which all ideas were encouraged and documented without immedi-
ate evaluation. This approach aimed to promote creativity and ensure a wide range of possible
solutions, thereby reducing the risk of overlooking viable alternatives due to early fixation on a
specific concept.

Following the brainstorming phase, the identified sub-functions and their respective solutions
were structured in morphological matrices to enable systematic combination of the sub-solutions
into complete concepts. To avoid generating an excessive number of impractical concepts, in-
compatible or unrealistic combinations were excluded during the process. Sub-solutions that
were not feasible in combination with other elements were removed entirely from further con-
sideration.


2.4.2  Concept Screening and Scoring


To ensure that the most suitable solutions were carried forward in the concept evaluation, the
selection was conducted using multiple matrices. These matrices were based on the requirements
previously defined for the solution.


2.4.2.1  Elimination Matrix


The concepts generated from the morphological matrix were evaluated using an elimination
matrix, in which each concept was assessed against the requirements defined in the requirements
specification. Concepts that failed to satisfy any of the mandatory requirements were directly
excluded.  In cases where compliance was uncertain, the concepts were set aside for further
investigation before a final decision was made.





8                                                                                         2. Methods


2.4.2.2  Pugh Matrix


The concepts that passed the elimination stage were further evaluated using Pugh matrices. In
this method, the concepts were compared against each other based on selected evaluation crite-
ria derived from the requirements specification. Multiple Pugh matrices were constructed using
different reference concepts, providing a more robust basis for comparison and supporting in-
formed decision-making.


2.5  Verification of Solution


The final step in ensuring that the solutions met all the specified requirements was to verify their
functionality. This was carried out in a similar manner to the evaluation of the existing solution
in Section 2.3, using static mechanical simulations. In addition, all component data sheets and
the bill of materials (BOM) were reviewed to ensure that the solution complied with and fulfilled
the defined requirements.

           Preliminary Study




To gain a clearer understanding of the problem, a preliminary study was conducted.  It began
with interviews with relevant stakeholders and industry professionals, followed by a state-of-
the-art review. This was succeeded by a technical analysis focusing on overpressure and leak
rate. Finally, today’s design of the solution was examined in greater detail.


3.1  Interviews


Four interviews were conducted, with the first and most extensive one being with Permanova.
The three subsequent interviews were held with a company that offers sealing solutions for
applications such as cleanrooms, the supplier of passive panels used by Permanova, and finally,
a staff member from the cleanroom facility at Chalmers.


3.1.1  Permanova


The first interview was conducted with Permanova, as they possessed the most comprehensive
information regarding today’s solution, its limitations, and the goals for the new design. Ad-
ditional questions were asked to clarify why the problem exists, how it originated, and why it
is necessary to fill the entire room with argon. Continuous communication with the company
was maintained throughout the project whenever further questions arose or clarifications were
needed.

The most critical takeaways from the Permanova interview concerned the enclosure being re-
quired to keep an overpressure with an inflow of 283 litre per minute (LPM), hence the maxi-
mum leak rate allowed is 283 LPM. Other important insights included a deeper understanding
of today’s solution, its lifespan, material usage, and the importance of complying with Swedish
workplace regulations.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM), particularly laser-based powder bed fusion (PBF-LB), enables the production of high-strength, lightweight components made of aluminum alloys such as AlSi10Mg. However, joining these parts via welding remains a significant challenge due to weld seam porosity caused by hydrogen entrapment. This study investigated the influence of the PBF-LB process parameters, tungsten inert gas (TIG) welding settings, filler material, and post-weld T6 heat treatment on the tensile strength and porosity of welded AlSi10Mg components. Using two different layer heights (30 µm and 60 µm), plate thicknesses (3 mm and 5 mm), and varying welding conditions, a series of 10 TIG-welded sample groups were fabricated and analyzed. Microstructural, hardness, porosity, and tensile tests revealed that porosity was high across all samples (11–19%). A subsequent T6 heat treatment improved the tensile strength. Higher layer heights and thinner plates led to a higher tensile strength of the weld seam, while the addition of a filler material showed limited benefits. No other influencing factors or interactions could be found. The results emphasize the need to optimize hydrogen control in the processes, melt pool dynamics, and weld seam geometry to receive reliable joints in lightweight manufacturing of PBF-LB AlSi10Mg parts.</jats:p>

Victor Lubkowitz, Leonie Fayner, Steffen Kramer, Volker Schulze, and Frederik Zanger. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procir.2024.08.086, doi:10.1016/j.procir.2024.08.086. This article has 3 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt concerns moisture reduction in AlSi10Mg powder for laser powder bed fusion and compares furnace, vacuum, and in-process laser drying. Moisture increases when powder contacts humid air, and moisture-derived oxygen can promote aluminum oxide/hydroxide formation, contributing to pore formation and reduced component density. The reported experiments measure powder moisture before and after drying using Karl Fischer titration, although the excerpt does not provide the resulting moisture values in ppm or wt% or a direct hydrogen-content value for the aluminum powder. Furnace drying conditions listed in the table include 80, 120, 160, and 200 °C; the excerpt does not state corresponding furnace holding times. Vacuum drying settings include examples designated V5/25/600/5 and V20/80/60/20, apparently encoding pressure, temperature, holding time, and cycles, but the table formatting is incomplete in the excerpt. In-process laser drying uses a defocused 1070 nm beam and low power, with listed settings including 75 W, 1000–1500 mm/s, and energy volumes of 0.155–0.16 J/mm³. All methods reduce moisture, but in-process drying is described as most effective. Furnace and vacuum drying can grow oxide layers and produce worse final density, whereas low-energy laser drying best reduces hydrogen pores and increases density. Prior cited work found air drying at 100 °C for up to 60 minutes increased density, and both laser and furnace drying reduced hydrogen pore density.

## pqac-00000032

From text 'lubkowitz2024comparisonofinprocess pages 4-5'.

Victor Lubkowitz, Leonie Fayner, Steffen Kramer, Volker Schulze, and Frederik Zanger. Comparison of in-process laser drying with furnace and vacuum drying to reduce moisture of alsi10mg powder processed in laser powder bed fusion. Procedia CIRP, Oct 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procir.2024.08.086, doi:10.1016/j.procir.2024.08.086. This article has 3 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt compares furnace, vacuum, and in-process laser drying of AlSi10Mg powder, but it does not provide numerical powder moisture content in ppm or wt%, hydrogen concentration in the powder, or specific furnace/vacuum drying temperatures and times. It reports that in-process laser drying provides the strongest moisture reduction, while furnace drying has the weakest effect. Vacuum-dried powder can produce higher sample density than oven-dried powder, probably because its oxide layer is thinner; however, longer vacuum retention and insufficient moisture removal can promote oxide-layer growth. The key effect on hydrogen porosity is observed with laser drying: hydrogen pores decrease from 28% in undried powder to 9% at a laser drying energy density of 3.9 J/mm³ and to 3% at 9.6 J/mm³. The validity of the 3% result is questioned because high-energy processing also causes lack-of-fusion porosity. Laser energy must be limited, since energies above 3.9 J/mm³ can sinter powder particles, producing a brittle coherent layer, increased surface roughness, and impaired component build-up. Overall, none of the methods restored the powder to the density performance of new powder. The authors conclude that moisture cannot be fully removed from highly oxidation-sensitive AlSi10Mg using the tested methods and suggest an inert, closed powder cycle.

The excerpt describes two methods for generating an LPBF process atmosphere: vacuum purge and simple purge. In a vacuum purge, the chamber is evacuated to remove most of the initial air and then backfilled with inert gas, typically argon or nitrogen. The evacuation and backfill sequence may be repeated until the required purity is reached. In a simple purge, the chamber is not evacuated; inert gas dilutes the initial air until the desired residual oxygen concentration is achieved, and this is identified as the most commonly adopted technique. After the oxygen requirement specified by the machine manufacturer is met, the gas is generally recirculated through filters that remove particles, while feedback control establishes the gas speed. The text warns that measured oxygen concentration depends on sensor type, calibration, and sensor position relative to the powder bed. However, this excerpt does not provide the requested numerical information for an EOS M290 or Renishaw system: it gives no number of purge cycles required to reach below 100 ppm oxygen, no purge flow rate, no chamber or gas-consumption volume, and no manufacturer-specific vacuum-purge procedure.

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Machine/System | Purge Method | O₂ Setpoint/Achieved | Purge Flow/Duration | Key Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| NIST AMMT | Vacuum evacuation, then N₂ or Ar backfill | Not reported in the cited design paper | Evacuation capability to approximately 0.1 Pa (10⁻³ mbar); cycle time not reported | Medium-vacuum chamber was selected to reduce O₂ faster than displacement purging alone; vacuum-induced chamber deflection required mechanical decoupling of the optics (pqac-00000024) |
| EOS M290 | High-flow displacement purge followed by closed-loop recirculation and a small make-up flow | Machine-defined start threshold; approximately 1000 ppm is a commonly reported LPBF start threshold, not a guaranteed EOS M290 specification | Approximately 40 L/min for 20 min, or about 800 L of supplied gas; a few L/min during printing | Gas consumption and attained purity depend on chamber volume, tightness, mixing and sensor location (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000053) |
| TRUMPF TruPrint1000 | Ar flushing and recirculation; external ADDvance O₂ precision control used in the cited experiment | 100 ppm target; external electrochemical system maintained approximately 100 ppm | Not reported | Used Ar 5.0; the standard machine lambda probe and external electrochemical sensor can disagree because the hot zirconia probe is cross-sensitive to reducing gases such as H₂ (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000018) |
| Renishaw AM250 | Evacuation followed by Ar purge; recirculation through the filter after purging | O₂ target not reported in the cited moisture study | Not reported | The study compared evacuation-plus-purge with purge-only operation and monitored chamber RH; filter condition materially affected residual moisture (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000051) |

{"answer": "## Atmosphere Control and Seal Design for a Vacuum-Purged LPBF Chamber Processing Aluminium Alloys: A Literature Review

### 1. Residual O₂ and H₂O Levels, Purging Strategies, and Published Machine Data

**Vacuum purging versus flow purging.** Two principal methods exist for establishing the inert atmosphere in an LPBF build chamber. Flow (displacement) purging uses elevated inert-gas flow to dilute and displace the initial air until the residual oxygen falls below a machine-defined threshold; it is the most commonly adopted commercial approach (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000052). Vacuum purging evacuates most of the air before back-filling with inert gas, optionally repeating the cycle; it has not been broadly adopted by equipment manufacturers despite its potential for faster and more gas-efficient atmosphere preparation (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000053). For an ideal well-mixed chamber evacuated to 1 mbar and backfilled with Ar 5.0 (≤10 ppm total impurities), a single cycle reduces atmospheric O₂ from approximately 210,000 ppm to roughly 210 ppm; two cycles bring it below approximately 0.2 ppm from the residual air contribution alone, with leaks, outgassing, and gas-supply impurities dominating thereafter.

**Published machine data.** Approximately 1,000 ppm O₂ (0.1%) is the typical process-initiation threshold for most commercial LPBF systems (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003). The EOS M290, a widely studied platform, uses approximately 40 L/min of inert gas during chamber purging for about 20 minutes (approximately 800 L total), followed by a holding flow of a few L/min during printing to counteract leaks (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000053). The TRUMPF TruPrint1000 was operated in one study with an Argon 5.0 supply and a target of 100 ppm O₂, which the external ADDvance O₂ precision electrochemical system achieved and maintained stably (pqac-00000002). The Renishaw AM250, a system that includes evacuation capability, was studied with both evacuation-plus-argon-purge and purge-only preparation; the study primarily monitored chamber relative humidity rather than reporting a specific O₂ endpoint (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000051). The NIST Additive Manufacturing Metrology Testbed (AMMT) uses a medium-vacuum chamber capable of reaching approximately 0.1 Pa (10⁻³ torr), enabling vacuum purging prior to backfilling with nitrogen or argon, which the designers note "provides faster means to reduce oxygen levels compared to simply purging with inert gas" (pqac-00000024). The AMMT optics tower is mechanically decoupled from the vacuum chamber to avoid deflection-induced alignment errors (pqac-00000025).

**Leak rates and rate-of-rise.** Quantitative leak-rate specifications (mbar·L/s) for commercial LPBF machines are not routinely published in the open literature. The Karlsson study on a pressurized build chamber enclosure noted that the maximum allowable leak rate was defined by the available inert gas supply—283 L/min in that case—illustrating that large-format machine enclosures are typically designed for positive-pressure containment rather than vacuum tightness (pqac-00000030). For a 6–10 L chamber with O-ring face seals and KF-25 flanges designed for evacuation to 1 mbar, well-assembled FKM seals on clean, properly finished flanges should readily achieve integral leak rates below 10⁻⁴ mbar·L/s, which is orders of magnitude tighter than what is achievable with panel-based enclosures. A rate-of-rise test—isolating the pumped-down chamber and monitoring pressure increase over time—is the standard acceptance method; the resulting rate directly gives the total leak-plus-outgassing load in mbar·L/s.

The following table summarizes published purging strategies and oxygen levels for representative LPBF systems:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2. O₂ and Moisture Thresholds for Processing Aluminium Alloys

**Oxygen thresholds.** Aluminium alloys are particularly susceptible to oxidation due to the thermodynamic stability of Al₂O₃. Many LPBF studies processing Al alloys (AlSi10Mg, 2xxx, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr) report maintaining chamber O₂ below 100 ppm (pqac-00000002). Baroutaji et al. (2023) systematically compared AlSi10Mg fabricated at 100 ppm and 1,000 ppm O₂ on an EOS M290 and found relatively modest macroscopic effects: elongation improved by approximately 5.7% at lower oxygen, while ultimate tensile strength decreased by approximately 3% and yield stress by approximately 1% (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008). For TPMS lattice structures, compressive property variations were generally below 2–8% depending on geometry (pqac-00000010). The authors characterized their findings as preliminary and recommended investigating a broader range including 20–2,000 ppm (pqac-00000005).

**Oxide inclusions and fatigue.** Tang (2017) demonstrated that in LPBF AlSi10Mg, oxide-driven pores were the dominant defect controlling fatigue resistance (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040). Larger oxide particles associated with crack initiation were believed to form through oxidation of metal vapor during manufacture. While oxide inclusions were observed to be smaller than the dominant pores, they were found on fracture surfaces at fatigue-failure initiation sites. Lack-of-fusion pores with sharp edges created the strongest stress concentrations and were the most harmful to fatigue life (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042).

**Hydrogen porosity.** The mechanism linking moisture to hydrogen porosity is well established: ambient moisture reacts with liquid aluminium at melt-pool temperatures to form Al₂O₃ and atomic hydrogen, which dissolves readily in the melt but has dramatically lower solubility in the solid, leading to pore nucleation during solidification (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000035). Van Cauwenbergh (2019) reported that LPBF AlSi7Mg0.6 printed at approximately 3 ppm O₂ with process gas containing ≤5 ppm H₂O produced parts with 13 ± 4 ppm hydrogen versus 45 ± 11 ppm in the starting powder, indicating significant hydrogen loss during the vacuum pre-cycle and printing (pqac-00000036). Elevated oxygen and moisture in the atmosphere promote oxidation and balling: reducing oxygen from 2% to 0.1% was shown to prevent balling in 316L through reduced melt-pool oxidation and improved wettability (pqac-00000007).

**Spatter.** Higher oxygen concentrations contribute to oxide-film stabilization on the melt pool, which can alter surface-tension-driven flow, increase spatter generation, and change spatter morphology. The recirculation of spatter-contaminated powder, which carries higher oxygen, can progressively degrade powder quality and increase porosity in subsequent layers (pqac-00000007).

### 3. Seal Design for Vacuum Plus Low Positive Pressure

**O-ring permeation: FKM versus other elastomers.** Sturm et al. (2004) measured permeation coefficients for polymer O-rings used in gas-sampling flasks. For Viton (FKM), the O₂ permeation coefficient was approximately 1.0–1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m²·s⁻¹·hPa⁻¹, while NBR ranged from 0.7 to 6.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m²·s⁻¹·hPa⁻¹ in the same units (pqac-00000015). Silicone was substantially more permeable, with values in the range of 76–460 × 10⁻¹⁵ m²·s⁻¹·hPa⁻¹. For water vapor, FKM had a permeation coefficient of approximately 220 × 10⁻¹⁵ m²·s⁻¹·hPa⁻¹, which is much higher than its O₂ permeation, confirming that water-vapor permeation through elastomeric seals is a significant contributor to chamber moisture even when O₂ leakage is well controlled (pqac-00000016). The authors noted that polymer formulation and manufacturer differences can produce order-of-magnitude variation in permeation coefficients (pqac-00000015).

**Implications for a 2.3 m seal length.** For 2.3 m of FKM O-ring seal (e.g., 3.53 mm cross-section compressed to approximately 2.5 mm exposed width), a crude estimate of the O₂ permeation flux at atmospheric ΔpO₂ of approximately 210 hPa across a compressed thickness of approximately 2 mm gives an O₂ ingress rate on the order of 10⁻⁴ mbar·L/s, which would add roughly 0.5–1 ppm/hour to a 10 L chamber at 1013 mbar—generally acceptable. Water vapor, with a permeation coefficient approximately 200× higher, would dominate the seal-permeation contribution to chamber humidity.

**O-ring gland design.** For vacuum-plus-low-positive-pressure service, standard AS568/ISO 3601 gland dimensions with 15–25% squeeze and gland fill of 70–85% are appropriate. The surface finish for vacuum-grade O-ring grooves is typically Ra ≤ 0.4 µm on the sealing surfaces. KF-25 flanges with centering rings and FKM O-rings are well-suited for this pressure regime.

**Outgassing.** FKM has lower outgassing rates than NBR, EPDM, or silicone, which is an important consideration for vacuum chambers. Aluminium walls outgas primarily water vapor; baking at modest temperatures (100–150°C) dramatically reduces outgassing rates, but the 200°C build plate in an LPBF chamber will warm nearby surfaces and can drive desorption of adsorbed water from internal chamber walls, increasing the moisture load (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000026).

**Dynamic seals for the build piston and recoater.** The NIST AMMT uses a "spring/felt seal assembly" around the build plate, which is noted in descriptions of the build bed, powder feed, and recoater alignment system, although specific seal-geometry details are not provided (pqac-00000025). Felt and brush seals provide powder containment while accommodating the sliding motion of the build piston; they do not provide high-integrity gas sealing and are typically complemented by an O-ring or PTFE lip seal on the piston rod for atmosphere containment. Edge-welded metal bellows can provide zero-leak dynamic sealing for limited strokes but are expensive and must be protected from powder ingress. Magnetic-fluid (ferrofluidic) feedthroughs are well-established for rotary shaft sealing in vacuum applications and provide leak rates below 10⁻⁹ mbar·L/s, making them attractive for a recoater shaft feedthrough where rotary motion must pass through the chamber wall without compromising atmosphere quality. Standard PTFE lip seals on a rotary shaft offer leak rates in the 10⁻³ to 10⁻² mbar·L/s range, which may be adequate for a positive-pressure chamber but would dominate the leak budget of a vacuum-purged system.

### 4. Oxygen Sensors for LPBF

The comparison between sensor technologies in an LPBF environment is summarized in the following table:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Key finding from LPBF-specific comparison.** Pauzon et al. (2021) directly compared a zirconia-based lambda probe (the standard sensor in the TRUMPF TruPrint1000) with an electrochemical cell (ADDvance O₂ precision) during LPBF processing of Ti-6Al-4V. When the lambda probe recorded a 50 ppm O₂ increase, the electrochemical cell simultaneously measured a 700 ppm increase—a 14:1 discrepancy attributed to the lambda probe's cross-sensitivity to hydrogen and other reducing species (H₂, CO) that oxidize on the hot (approximately 700°C) sensor head, consuming oxygen and making the reading appear artificially low (pqac-00000018). The electrochemical cell does not exhibit this cross-sensitivity. Over seven hours of continuous monitoring, the electrochemical sensor measured an oxygen drift of approximately 1.7 ppm O₂/min, providing a direct measure of the total leak-plus-outgassing-plus-permeation rate of the system (pqac-00000018).

**Response time.** Electrochemical and semiconductor metal oxide sensors exhibit response times ranging from approximately 3–4 seconds to 60–70 seconds depending on electrolyte composition, electrode design, temperature, and sampling geometry (pqac-00000020). Heated planar zirconia sensors can reach operating temperature in under 10 seconds, but installed sampling-line dead volume typically dominates system response (pqac-00000021).

**Poisoning.** Zirconia sensors are susceptible to poisoning by sulfur oxides at concentrations as low as a few ppm, and by lead and phosphorus compounds that can coat electrode surfaces (pqac-00000020). In an LPBF environment, metal condensate, soot, and silicone-derived contamination (from greases, sealants, or silicone-based thermal interface materials) represent analogous poisoning risks; locating the sensor in a filtered sample bypass is essential (pqac-00000020). Electrochemical cells are sensitive to membrane fouling and electrolyte ageing and require periodic replacement.

**Dew-point sensors.** Chamber humidity in LPBF has been monitored using capacitive probe hygrometers measuring relative humidity, as demonstrated on the Renishaw AM250 (pqac-00000051). Chilled-mirror dew-point sensors provide a primary measurement of water content and are suitable for monitoring the LPBF chamber gas, though their use in LPBF has not been widely reported in the literature.

### 5. Moisture Carried by Aluminium Alloy Powders, Drying Practice, and Effects

**Powder moisture content.** Lubkowitz et al. (2024) measured new AlSi10Mg powder at 0.015 wt% (approximately 150 ppm by mass) moisture using Karl Fischer titration; this condition yielded the highest achievable component density of 2.65 ± 0.002 g/cm³ (pqac-00000037). Storage in unsealed containers or exposure to humid air increased moisture and reduced achievable density. Van Cauwenbergh (2019) reported that AlSi7Mg0.6 powder contained 45 ± 11 ppm hydrogen, while printed parts contained 13 ± 4 ppm, with the reduction attributed partly to moisture extraction during the vacuum pre-cycle and to low-moisture process gas (H₂O ≤ 5 ppm) (pqac-00000036). Cordova et al. (2017) found that aluminium powders (Scalmalloy and AlSi10Mg) were the most moisture-sensitive among the alloys tested (also including Ti-6Al-4V, IN718, 316L), with AlSi10Mg showing the strongest visual and compositional response to humid aging at 50°C, 80% RH for 72 hours (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034). Schulze et al. (2025) reported hydrogen contents ranging from 143 to 908 ppm in AlSi10Mg powder depending on condition (new, briefly aged, aged, or aged plus dried) (pqac-00000037).

**Drying practice.** Cordova et al. (2017) used vacuum drying at 85°C for 6 hours and air drying at 150°C for 20 minutes (pqac-00000033). Lubkowitz et al. (2024) compared furnace drying at 80–200°C, vacuum drying (various pressure/temperature/time combinations), and in-process laser drying. Furnace drying had the weakest moisture-removal effect and can promote oxide layer growth, while vacuum-dried powder produced higher sample density than oven-dried powder, likely because its oxide layer was thinner (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032). In-process laser drying was most effective, reducing hydrogen pore fraction from 28% in undried powder to 9% at a laser energy density of 3.9 J/mm³ and to 3% at 9.6 J/mm³, though excessive energy caused particle sintering and lack-of-fusion defects (pqac-00000032). None of the methods fully restored aged powder to the density performance of new powder, leading the authors to recommend an inert, closed powder-handling cycle (pqac-00000032). Pre-drying at 200°C for 16 hours has also been reported to reduce pore enlargement during post-build heat treatment (pqac-00000037).

**Cellulosic filter as a moisture source.** Das et al. (2019) identified cellulosic HEPA-type filters used in LPBF recirculation systems as a significant unrecognized moisture source. A Hengst E1900 L filter stored at ambient humidity could retain up to 51.28 g of moisture (at 80% RH), which was subsequently released into the build chamber during inert-gas recirculation (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000050). Greater moisture desorption occurred during inert-gas purging than during evacuation, because the flowing gas enhanced desorption from the filter media (pqac-00000047). The recommended countermeasure is to dry the filter at 90°C for 5 hours before installation, which removed all measured moisture, or to store filters in a low-RH environment (pqac-00000050). This finding is directly relevant to the described chamber design, which uses a recirculating blower and HEPA filter: the filter can release grams of water into the chamber and significantly elevate the dew point unless it is properly conditioned.

**Effect on chamber dew point and hydrogen porosity.** The moisture released from powder, chamber walls, and especially from cellulosic filters establishes the chamber dew point, which is typically not monitored in commercial LPBF systems (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000049). At melt-pool temperatures, moisture dissociates to provide both oxygen (forming Al₂O₃) and hydrogen (dissolving into liquid aluminium). The sharp drop in hydrogen solubility during solidification nucleates hydrogen pores, which can grow further during post-build heat treatment, particularly at temperatures above 500°C where hydrogen diffusion becomes rapid (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000035). Controlling the chamber dew point through vacuum purging, dry gas supply, pre-dried filters, and dried powder is therefore essential for minimizing hydrogen porosity in LPBF aluminium alloys.

### Summary of Practical Implications for the Described 6–10 L Chamber

For a bare 6061-T6 aluminium chamber of 6–10 L with FKM O-ring face seals (2.3 m total), KF-25 flanges, and vacuum capability to approximately 1 mbar, the following design considerations emerge from this review:

1. **Vacuum purging** to 1 mbar followed by backfill with Ar 5.0 provides a theoretical single-cycle dilution of approximately 1000:1, reducing atmospheric O₂ from 210,000 ppm to approximately 210 ppm; a second cycle reaches sub-ppm residual air. This is significantly more efficient than flow purging, which requires approximately 800 L (or approximately 100 chamber volumes for a 10 L chamber) on an EOS M290 (pqac-00000053). The NIST AMMT adopted vacuum capability for this reason (pqac-00000024).

2. **FKM O-rings** provide the lowest gas permeation among common elastomers (O₂ permeation approximately 100× lower than silicone), but water-vapor permeation through FKM remains significant at approximately 220 × 10⁻¹⁵ m²·s⁻¹·hPa⁻¹ (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). An aluminium chamber will outgas primarily water vapor, and the 200°C build plate will accelerate wall desorption.

3. **Oxygen monitoring** should use an electrochemical cell rather than relying solely on a zirconia lambda probe, which can underestimate O₂ by an order of magnitude in the presence of hydrogen from moisture decomposition (pqac-00000018). The measured drift rate of approximately 1.7 ppm O₂/min from the electrochemical sensor provides a direct measure of total atmospheric ingress.

4. **Powder and filter conditioning** are critical: new AlSi10Mg powder carries approximately 150 ppm moisture (pqac-00000037), and cellulosic filters can hold tens of grams of water (pqac-00000050). Pre-drying the powder and filter before each build is essential for minimizing hydrogen porosity.

5. **Target atmosphere quality** for aluminium alloy processing should aim for ≤100 ppm O₂ and dew point below −40°C (approximately 120 ppm H₂O), based on the thresholds used in research studies achieving high-density, low-porosity parts (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000036)."}

### 2. O₂ and Moisture Thresholds for Processing Aluminium Alloys

Many LPBF studies processing Al alloys (AlSi10Mg, 2xxx, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr) report maintaining chamber O₂ below 100 ppm (pqac-00000002). Baroutaji et al. For TPMS lattice structures, compressive property variations were generally below 2–8% depending on geometry (pqac-00000010). The authors characterized their findings as preliminary and recommended investigating a broader range including 20–2,000 ppm (pqac-00000005).

Larger oxide particles associated with crack initiation were believed to form through oxidation of metal vapor during manufacture. While oxide inclusions were observed to be smaller than the dominant pores, they were found on fracture surfaces at fatigue-failure initiation sites. Lack-of-fusion pores with sharp edges created the strongest stress concentrations and were the most harmful to fatigue life (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042).

**Hydrogen porosity.** The mechanism linking moisture to hydrogen porosity is well established: ambient moisture reacts with liquid aluminium at melt-pool temperatures to form Al₂O₃ and atomic hydrogen, which dissolves readily in the melt but has dramatically lower solubility in the solid, leading to pore nucleation during solidification (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000035). Silicone was substantially more permeable, with values in the range of 76–460 × 10⁻¹⁵ m²·s⁻¹·hPa⁻¹. The authors noted that polymer formulation and manufacturer differences can produce order-of-magnitude variation in permeation coefficients (pqac-00000015).

**Key finding from LPBF-specific comparison.** Pauzon et al. Silicone was substantially more permeable, with values in the range of 76–460 × 10⁻¹⁵ m²·s⁻¹·hPa⁻¹. For water vapor, FKM had a permeation coefficient of approximately 220 × 10⁻¹⁵ m²·s⁻¹·hPa⁻¹, which is much higher than its O₂ permeation, confirming that water-vapor permeation through elastomeric seals is a significant contributor to chamber moisture even when O₂ leakage is well controlled (sturm2004permeationofatmospheric pages 4-6). The authors noted that polymer formulation and manufacturer differences can produce order-of-magnitude variation in permeation coefficients (sturm2004permeationofatmospheric pages 3-4).

**Implications for a 2.3 m seal length.** For 2.3 m of FKM O-ring seal (e.g., 3.53 mm cross-section compressed to approximately 2.5 mm exposed width), a crude estimate of the O₂ permeation flux at atmospheric ΔpO₂ of approximately 210 hPa across a compressed thickness of approximately 2 mm gives an O₂ ingress rate on the order of 10⁻⁴ mbar·L/s, which would add roughly 0.5–1 ppm/hour to a 10 L chamber at 1013 mbar—generally acceptable. Water vapor, with a permeation coefficient approximately 200× higher, would dominate the seal-permeation contribution to chamber humidity.

**O-ring gland design.** For vacuum-plus-low-positive-pressure service, standard AS568/ISO 3601 gland dimensions with 15–25% squeeze and gland fill of 70–85% are appropriate. The surface finish for vacuum-grade O-ring grooves is typically Ra ≤ 0.4 µm on the sealing surfaces. KF-25 flanges with centering rings and FKM O-rings are well-suited for this pressure regime.

**Outgassing.** FKM has lower outgassing rates than NBR, EPDM, or silicone, which is an important consideration for vacuum chambers. Aluminium walls outgas primarily water vapor; baking at modest temperatures (100–150°C) dramatically reduces outgassing rates, but the 200°C build plate in an LPBF chamber will warm nearby surfaces and can drive desorption of adsorbed water from internal chamber walls, increasing the moisture load (pauzon2019theprocessatmosphere pages 22-25, das2020moisturesourcesin pages 25-66).

Felt and brush seals provide powder containment while accommodating the sliding motion of the build piston; they do not provide high-integrity gas sealing and are typically complemented by an O-ring or PTFE lip seal on the piston rod for atmosphere containment. Edge-welded metal bellows can provide zero-leak dynamic sealing for limited strokes but are expensive and must be protected from powder ingress. Magnetic-fluid (ferrofluidic) feedthroughs are well-established for rotary shaft sealing in vacuum applications and provide leak rates below 10⁻⁹ mbar·L/s, making them attractive for a recoater shaft feedthrough where rotary motion must pass through the chamber wall without compromising atmosphere quality. Standard PTFE lip seals on a rotary shaft offer leak rates in the 10⁻³ to 10⁻² mbar·L/s range, which may be adequate for a positive-pressure chamber but would dominate the leak budget of a vacuum-purged system.

Storage in unsealed containers or exposure to humid air increased moisture and reduced achievable density. Van Cauwenbergh (2019) reported that AlSi7Mg0.6 powder contained 45 ± 11 ppm hydrogen, while printed parts contained 13 ± 4 ppm, with the reduction attributed partly to moisture extraction during the vacuum pre-cycle and to low-moisture process gas (H₂O ≤ 5 ppm) (cauwenbergh2019reducinghydrogenporesb pages 4-6). Cordova et al. (2017) found that aluminium powders (Scalmalloy and AlSi10Mg) were the most moisture-sensitive among the alloys tested (also including Ti-6Al-4V, IN718, 316L), with AlSi10Mg showing the strongest visual and compositional response to humid aging at 50°C, 80% RH for 72 hours (cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 1-3, cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 3-5). Schulze et al. (2025) reported hydrogen contents ranging from 143 to 908 ppm in AlSi10Mg powder depending on condition (new, briefly aged, aged, or aged plus dried) (lubkowitz2024comparisonofinprocess pages 5-6).

None of the methods fully restored aged powder to the density performance of new powder, leading the authors to recommend an inert, closed powder-handling cycle (lubkowitz2024comparisonofinprocess pages 4-5). Pre-drying at 200°C for 16 hours has also been reported to reduce pore enlargement during post-build heat treatment (lubkowitz2024comparisonofinprocess pages 5-6).

Greater moisture desorption occurred during inert-gas purging than during evacuation, because the flowing gas enhanced desorption from the filter media (das2019contributionofcellulosic pages 5-6). The recommended countermeasure is to dry the filter at 90°C for 5 hours before installation, which removed all measured moisture, or to store filters in a low-RH environment (das2019contributionofcellulosic pages 6-7). This finding is directly relevant to the described chamber design, which uses a recirculating blower and HEPA filter: the filter can release grams of water into the chamber and significantly elevate the dew point unless it is properly conditioned.

**Effect on chamber dew point and hydrogen porosity.** The moisture released from powder, chamber walls, and especially from cellulosic filters establishes the chamber dew point, which is typically not monitored in commercial LPBF systems (das2020moisturesourcesina pages 66-116, das2019contributionofcellulosic pages 1-2). At melt-pool temperatures, moisture dissociates to provide both oxygen (forming Al₂O₃) and hydrogen (dissolving into liquid aluminium). The sharp drop in hydrogen solubility during solidification nucleates hydrogen pores, which can grow further during post-build heat treatment, particularly at temperatures above 500°C where hydrogen diffusion becomes rapid (kramer2026investigationofthe pages 2-4). Controlling the chamber dew point through vacuum purging, dry gas supply, pre-dried filters, and dried powder is therefore essential for minimizing hydrogen porosity in LPBF aluminium alloys.

### Summary of Practical Implications for the Described 6–10 L Chamber

For a bare 6061-T6 aluminium chamber of 6–10 L with FKM O-ring face seals (2.3 m total), KF-25 flanges, and vacuum capability to approximately 1 mbar, the following design considerations emerge from this review:

1. **Vacuum purging** to 1 mbar followed by backfill with Ar 5.0 provides a theoretical single-cycle dilution of approximately 1000:1, reducing atmospheric O₂ from 210,000 ppm to approximately 210 ppm; a second cycle reaches sub-ppm residual air. This is significantly more efficient than flow purging, which requires approximately 800 L (or approximately 100 chamber volumes for a 10 L chamber) on an EOS M290 (pauzon2021tailoredprocessgases pages 23-26). The NIST AMMT adopted vacuum capability for this reason (lane2016designdevelopmentsand pages 3-6).

2. **FKM O-rings** provide the lowest gas permeation among common elastomers (O₂ permeation approximately 100× lower than silicone), but water-vapor permeation through FKM remains significant at approximately 220 × 10⁻¹⁵ m²·s⁻¹·hPa⁻¹ (sturm2004permeationofatmospheric pages 3-4, sturm2004permeationofatmospheric pages 4-6). An aluminium chamber will outgas primarily water vapor, and the 200°C build plate will accelerate wall desorption.

3. **Oxygen monitoring** should use an electrochemical cell rather than relying solely on a zirconia lambda probe, which can underestimate O₂ by an order of magnitude in the presence of hydrogen from moisture decomposition (pauzon2021controlofresidual pages 8-12). The measured drift rate of approximately 1.7 ppm O₂/min from the electrochemical sensor provides a direct measure of total atmospheric ingress.

4. **Powder and filter conditioning** are critical: new AlSi10Mg powder carries approximately 150 ppm moisture (lubkowitz2024comparisonofinprocess pages 5-6), and cellulosic filters can hold tens of grams of water (das2019contributionofcellulosic pages 6-7). Pre-drying the powder and filter before each build is essential for minimizing hydrogen porosity.

5. **Target atmosphere quality** for aluminium alloy processing should aim for ≤100 ppm O₂ and dew point below −40°C (approximately 120 ppm H₂O), based on the thresholds used in research studies achieving high-density, low-porosity parts (pauzon2021controlofresidual pages 3-6, cauwenbergh2019reducinghydrogenporesb pages 4-6).

### 1. Residual O₂ and H₂O Levels, Purging Strategies, and Published Machine Data

**Vacuum purging versus flow purging.** Two principal methods exist for establishing the inert atmosphere in an LPBF build chamber. Flow (displacement) purging uses elevated inert-gas flow to dilute and displace the initial air until the residual oxygen falls below a machine-defined threshold; it is the most commonly adopted commercial approach (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000052). Vacuum purging evacuates most of the air before back-filling with inert gas, optionally repeating the cycle; it has not been broadly adopted by equipment manufacturers despite its potential for faster and more gas-efficient atmosphere preparation (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000053). For an ideal well-mixed chamber evacuated to 1 mbar and backfilled with Ar 5.0 (≤10 ppm total impurities), a single cycle reduces atmospheric O₂ from approximately 210,000 ppm to roughly 210 ppm; two cycles bring it below approximately 0.2 ppm from the residual air contribution alone, with leaks, outgassing, and gas-supply impurities dominating thereafter.

**Published machine data.** Approximately 1,000 ppm O₂ (0.1%) is the typical process-initiation threshold for most commercial LPBF systems (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003). The EOS M290, a widely studied platform, uses approximately 40 L/min of inert gas during chamber purging for about 20 minutes (approximately 800 L total), followed by a holding flow of a few L/min during printing to counteract leaks (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000053). The TRUMPF TruPrint1000 was operated in one study with an Argon 5.0 supply and a target of 100 ppm O₂, which the external ADDvance O₂ precision electrochemical system achieved and maintained stably (pqac-00000002). The Renishaw AM250, a system that includes evacuation capability, was studied with both evacuation-plus-argon-purge and purge-only preparation; the study primarily monitored chamber relative humidity rather than reporting a specific O₂ endpoint (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000051). The NIST Additive Manufacturing Metrology Testbed (AMMT) uses a medium-vacuum chamber capable of reaching approximately 0.1 Pa (10⁻³ torr), enabling vacuum purging prior to backfilling with nitrogen or argon, which the designers note "provides faster means to reduce oxygen levels compared to simply purging with inert gas" (pqac-00000024). The AMMT optics tower is mechanically decoupled from the vacuum chamber to avoid deflection-induced alignment errors (pqac-00000025).

**Leak rates and rate-of-rise.** Quantitative leak-rate specifications (mbar·L/s) for commercial LPBF machines are not routinely published in the open literature. The Karlsson study on a pressurized build chamber enclosure noted that the maximum allowable leak rate was defined by the available inert gas supply—283 L/min in that case—illustrating that large-format machine enclosures are typically designed for positive-pressure containment rather than vacuum tightness (pqac-00000030). For a 6–10 L chamber with O-ring face seals and KF-25 flanges designed for evacuation to 1 mbar, well-assembled FKM seals on clean, properly finished flanges should readily achieve integral leak rates below 10⁻⁴ mbar·L/s, which is orders of magnitude tighter than what is achievable with panel-based enclosures. A rate-of-rise test—isolating the pumped-down chamber and monitoring pressure increase over time—is the standard acceptance method; the resulting rate directly gives the total leak-plus-outgassing load in mbar·L/s.
